synthesis.georgi-jarlskog-is-rung-vector.formal:
Work on the module $\Lambda^{\bullet}(W \oplus R_{2})$ of Proposition \claimref{synthesis.georgi-jarlskog-majorana-moment-map}, with $\beta_{i} = v_{i} \wedge w_{i} = n_{i} - \tfrac12$, $\mu_{P} = \tfrac18(\beta_{1} + \beta_{2} + \beta_{3})$, $\mu_{R} = \tfrac18(\beta_{4} + \beta_{5})$, $B - L = -\tfrac{16}{3}\mu_{P}$, $\chi = -(-1)^{N_{R}}$, $N_{P}$ the pair number, the Majorana element $T = v_{1}\cdots v_{5}$ of Proposition \claimref{standard-model.majorana-element}, $T_{\mathrm{GJ}} = w_{4}(B - L)\chi$ as in Proposition \claimref{families.doublet-direction-module-georgi-jarlskog-clebsch}, and mass forms $B(\psi, X\varphi)$ on the sixteen with the pairing of Lemma \claimref{standard-model.invariant-pairing-five-modes}. Here and below the sixteen is the particle half $(-1)^{N}$ of Proposition \claimref{standard-model.hyp-s-slot-statistics}, in which the empty state is $\nu^{c}$, the halving that the Pati-Salam stage of the chain forces (Theorem \claimref{synthesis.neutral-singlet-bit-decided-by-gauge-algebra-leaving-u5}(iii)); the Dirac-neutrino statements need that halving. Let $G_{4}$ be the degree-four part of $TT^{\dagger}$ in the Majorana monomials (Proposition \claimref{synthesis.georgi-jarlskog-square-of-majorana-element}), and split it by support into the pair-only part $P_{4}$, the pair-rung part $X_{4}$ and the rung-only part $R_{4}$. Then:
\begin{enumerate}
\item[(i)] \emph{(The split.)} $P_{4} = 4\mu_{P}^{2} - \tfrac{3}{64} = \tfrac{3}{64}\bigl(3(B - L)^{2} - 1\bigr) = \tfrac{3}{32}(B - L)(-1)^{N_{P}}$, which commutes with $\su(2)_{L}$, $\su(2)_{R}$, $\su(3)$ and $B - L$ but not with the pair bracket $v_{1}v_{2}$, so it lies in the $(15,1,1)$; $X_{4} = 8\mu_{R}\mu_{P}$, in the $(15,1,3)$ (stored); and $R_{4} = 4\mu_{R}^{2} - \tfrac{1}{32} = -\tfrac{1}{32}\chi$, the Pati-Salam singlet of Proposition \claimref{standard-model.automorphisms-preserve-slot-pair-split-are}.
\item[(ii)] \emph{(Pure Georgi-Jarlskog.)} On the sixteen $\chi = -(-1)^{N_{P}}$, so $w_{4}P_{4} = -\tfrac{3}{32}T_{\mathrm{GJ}}$ there, as operators. Its mass form is $-\tfrac{3}{32}$ times the Georgi-Jarlskog form, symmetric, with no antisymmetric ($120$) part and no $10$ component, $|y_{e}/y_{d}| = 3$; likewise $v_{4}P_{4}$ gives $-\tfrac{3}{32}$ times the up-type form of that proposition, $|m_{\nu}^{D}| = 3|m_{u}|$.
\item[(iii)] \emph{(Why $3$.)} For a weighting $f(B - L)$ of the rung vector, the even part of $f$ gives the symmetric form $x\,(10) + y\,(\mathrm{GJ})$ with $x = \tfrac14\bigl(3f(\tfrac13) + f(1)\bigr)$, a quarter of the trace of $f$ over a Pati-Salam quartet ($B - L = \tfrac13, \tfrac13, \tfrac13, -1$, Proposition \claimref{standard-model.generation-ten-under-pati-salam}), and $y = \tfrac34\bigl(f(\tfrac13) - f(1)\bigr)$, with no antisymmetric part; the odd part gives an antisymmetric form and no symmetric one, the grade-three form of Proposition \claimref{standard-model.grade-three-georgi-jarlskog-direction} for $f = B - L$. Pair-only Majorana monomials of degree two and four have zero trace on each pair-parity half of $\Lambda^{\bullet}W$ (each quartet); the degree-six one does not. Hence an even pair weighting gives the pure Georgi-Jarlskog form exactly when it is traceless on the quartet, as $P_{4}$ is.
\item[(iv)] \emph{(The square does not fix the coefficient.)} $w_{4}X_{4}$ gives $+\tfrac{3}{32}$ times the Georgi-Jarlskog form and $-\tfrac{3}{32}$ times the grade-three form (stored); $w_{4}R_{4}$ has no symmetric form; so the symmetric form of $w_{4}G_{4}$ vanishes identically. The scalar part of $TT^{\dagger}$ with the pair part, $w_{4}(\tfrac{1}{32} + P_{4})$, gives a lepton-only form, $\tfrac18$ of the $10$ form on $(L, e^{c})$ and zero on $(Q, d^{c})$.
\end{enumerate}
So the Georgi-Jarlskog operator is the rung vector times the $(15,1,1)$ part of the square of the Majorana element, at second order in a vev along $T$ and without the grade-three term that the $(15,1,3)$ composite carries; the factor $3$ is the quartet tracelessness of that part. The square, taken whole or truncated by degree, does not supply the weight of the $(15,1,1)$ part relative to the $10$; that weight is the open coefficient.
synthesis.georgi-jarlskog-is-rung-vector.technical: The problem asks whether one polynomial along the Majorana element fixes how strongly the $126$ enters the second family's mass relative to the $10$, and whether it produces the Georgi-Jarlskog factor $3$. The stored result found the Georgi-Jarlskog composite inside the square $TT^{\dagger}$ of the Majorana element as its pair-rung part, but with an equal-strength $120$ term attached. Here the remaining degree-four parts are computed. The pair-only part is a function of $B - L$ alone, and on the sixteen it equals $\tfrac{3}{32}(B - L)$ times the pair parity, which there is minus the rung parity; so the rung vector times it is exactly the Georgi-Jarlskog operator, with no $120$ and no $10$ part. The reason is a trace: any weighting of the rung coupling by a function of $B - L$ gives a $10$ part proportional to its trace over a Pati-Salam quartet, and the pair-space elements of degree two and four are traceless there. Given the square's own $(15,1,1)$ part, the factor $3$ therefore follows, with nothing fitted; which part a dynamics picks is open. The coefficient does not: the three degree-four parts give Georgi-Jarlskog terms that cancel, the whole degree-four component gives no symmetric mass at all, and keeping the scalar part alongside gives masses to leptons only. What a dynamics must supply is the weight of one Pati-Salam component of the square.
synthesis.georgi-jarlskog-is-rung-vector.lay: In this framework one hypothetical heavy object, the Majorana element, gives the right-handed neutrino its large mass. Squaring it produces several pieces that differ in how they transform under the larger symmetry of the model. One piece, combined with the ordinary Higgs coupling, produces exactly the classic three-to-one ratio between the masses of a charged lepton and a down-type quark, which the second family shows approximately when the masses are run to a high scale (a recollection from the literature, not used), and nothing else. Given that piece, the ratio three follows from the structure; which piece a dynamics picks is open. How strongly that piece enters, compared with the ordinary coupling, is still not decided by anything in the model.

proofs.main:
Notation as in the statement; $k$ denotes the pair number $N_{P}$ of a basis state, so that $\sum_{i \le 3}\beta_{i} = k - \tfrac32$, $\mu_{P} = \tfrac18(k - \tfrac32)$ and $B - L = 1 - \tfrac{2k}{3}$ on that state (Proposition \claimref{synthesis.georgi-jarlskog-majorana-moment-map}(i)).

(i) For the Majorana element $T$ of Proposition \claimref{standard-model.majorana-element}, by Proposition \claimref{synthesis.georgi-jarlskog-square-of-majorana-element}(i), $TT^{\dagger} = \prod_{i}(\tfrac12 + \beta_{i})$ and its degree-four part is $G_{4} = \tfrac18\sum_{i < l}\beta_{i}\beta_{l}$, each $\beta_{i}\beta_{l}$ ($i \ne l$) a single monomial of degree four supported on the modes $i$ and $l$. The pair-only part is $P_{4} = \tfrac18(\beta_{1}\beta_{2} + \beta_{1}\beta_{3} + \beta_{2}\beta_{3})$. Since $\beta_{i}^{2} = \tfrac14$, $P_{4} = \tfrac{1}{16}\bigl((\beta_{1} + \beta_{2} + \beta_{3})^{2} - \tfrac34\bigr) = \tfrac{1}{16}(64\mu_{P}^{2} - \tfrac34) = 4\mu_{P}^{2} - \tfrac{3}{64}$. With $\mu_{P} = -\tfrac{3}{16}(B - L)$, $4\mu_{P}^{2} = \tfrac{9}{64}(B - L)^{2}$, which gives $P_{4} = \tfrac{3}{64}(3(B - L)^{2} - 1)$. On the four values of $k$ this is $\tfrac{3}{32}, -\tfrac{1}{32}, -\tfrac{1}{32}, \tfrac{3}{32}$, and $(B - L)(-1)^{k}$ takes the values $1, -\tfrac13, -\tfrac13, 1$, so $P_{4} = \tfrac{3}{32}(B - L)(-1)^{N_{P}}$. The pair-rung part is $X_{4} = 8\mu_{R}\mu_{P}$ (loc. cit. (ii)). The rung-only part is $R_{4} = \tfrac18\beta_{4}\beta_{5}$; since $(-1)^{n_{4} + n_{5}} = (-2\beta_{4})(-2\beta_{5}) = 4\beta_{4}\beta_{5}$, $R_{4} = \tfrac{1}{32}(-1)^{N_{R}} = -\tfrac{1}{32}\chi$, and $4\mu_{R}^{2} - \tfrac{1}{32} = \tfrac{1}{16}(\tfrac12 + 2\beta_{4}\beta_{5}) - \tfrac{1}{32} = \tfrac18\beta_{4}\beta_{5}$. $P_{4}$ is a function of the pair occupations symmetric in the three pairs, so it commutes with $\su(3)$ (which preserves $k$ and permutes the pair occupations within each $k$), with $B - L$, and with every rung operator, hence with $\su(2)_{L}$ and $\su(2)_{R}$; the bracket $v_{1}v_{2}$ raises $k$ by two, between values $\tfrac{3}{32}$ and $-\tfrac{1}{32}$ ($k = 0 \to 2$), so $P_{4}$ does not commute with it. Degree-four monomials in the six pair generators span $\Lambda^{4}$ of the pair space, which under $\su(4)$ is the adjoint $15$ (it is $\Lambda^{2}$ times the pair volume element); with the commutation just shown, $P_{4}$ lies in the $(15,1,1)$. $R_{4}$ is a multiple of $\chi$, the Pati-Salam singlet of Proposition \claimref{standard-model.automorphisms-preserve-slot-pair-split-are}.

(ii) The sixteen are the states of even total number (the particle half of Proposition \claimref{standard-model.hyp-s-slot-statistics}, with $\nu^{c}$ the empty state, the halving forced by the Pati-Salam stage, Theorem \claimref{synthesis.neutral-singlet-bit-decided-by-gauge-algebra-leaving-u5}(iii)), so $(-1)^{N_{P}} = (-1)^{N_{R}} = -\chi$ on it. For $\varphi$ in the sixteen, $w_{4}P_{4}\varphi = \tfrac{3}{32}w_{4}(B - L)(-1)^{N_{P}}\varphi = -\tfrac{3}{32}w_{4}(B - L)\chi\varphi = -\tfrac{3}{32}T_{\mathrm{GJ}}\varphi$. The mass forms on the sixteen involve $X\varphi$ for $\varphi$ in the sixteen only, so the form of $w_{4}P_{4}$ is $-\tfrac{3}{32}$ times that of $T_{\mathrm{GJ}}$, which by Proposition \claimref{families.doublet-direction-module-georgi-jarlskog-clebsch}(i), (ii) is symmetric, is the $126$ component of $16 \otimes 16$ (no $10$, no $120$), and has $|y_{e}/y_{d}| = 3$. The same argument with $v_{4}$ and part (iv) of that proposition gives the up-type statement.

(iii) By Theorem \claimref{standard-model.yukawa-pattern-two-rung-module}, with the pairing of Lemma \claimref{standard-model.invariant-pairing-five-modes}, $w_{4}$ couples exactly $(L, e^{c})$ and $(Q, d^{c})$ and its form is symmetric; every coupled pair is $B - L$ neutral (Proposition \claimref{families.doublet-direction-module-georgi-jarlskog-clebsch}(iii)), with $|B - L| = 1$ on the lepton pair and $\tfrac13$ on the quark pair (Proposition \claimref{standard-model.generation-ten-under-pati-salam}). Since $f(B - L)$ is diagonal, $B(\psi, w_{4}f(B - L)\varphi) = f(q_{\varphi})B(\psi, w_{4}\varphi)$, and exchanging $\psi$ and $\varphi$ replaces $q_{\varphi}$ by $-q_{\varphi}$. So the symmetric part is the $10$ form weighted by the even part $f_{e}$ of $f$ (by $f_{e}(1)$ on leptons, $f_{e}(\tfrac13)$ on quarks) and the antisymmetric part the same with the odd part $f_{o}$. By (ii) the Georgi-Jarlskog form is the $10$ form weighted by $-1$ on leptons and $\tfrac13$ on quarks. Solving $f_{e}(1) = x - y$, $f_{e}(\tfrac13) = x + \tfrac{y}{3}$ gives $x = \tfrac14(3f_{e}(\tfrac13) + f_{e}(1))$, a quarter of the trace of $f_{e}$ over a quartet, and $y = \tfrac34(f_{e}(\tfrac13) - f_{e}(1))$. For $f = B - L$ the antisymmetric part is by definition the grade-three form of Proposition \claimref{standard-model.grade-three-georgi-jarlskog-direction}. For the traces: a pair monomial that is not a product of whole mode bivectors $a_{i}b_{i} = -2\beta_{i}$ changes some occupation and has zero diagonal. On the even half $\{\emptyset, \{1,2\}, \{1,3\}, \{2,3\}\}$, $\beta_{i}$ is $+\tfrac12$ on the two states containing $i$ and $-\tfrac12$ on the other two, so its trace is $0$; $\beta_{i}\beta_{l}$ ($i \ne l$) is $+\tfrac14$ on $\emptyset$ and on $\{i, l\}$ and $-\tfrac14$ on the other two, trace $0$; and similarly on the odd half by the particle-hole map $k \mapsto 3 - k$, which sends $\beta_{i}$ to $-\beta_{i}$. The degree-six product $\beta_{1}\beta_{2}\beta_{3}$ is $-\tfrac18$ on every state of the even half, trace $-\tfrac12 \ne 0$. $P_{4}$ is even in $B - L$ with $3P_{4}(\tfrac13) + P_{4}(1) = -\tfrac{3}{32} + \tfrac{3}{32} = 0$, so $x = 0$, as (ii) states.

(iv) $X_{4}$: Proposition \claimref{synthesis.georgi-jarlskog-square-of-majorana-element}(iii). $R_{4} = -\tfrac{1}{32}\chi$, and on each coupled pair one state is a doublet ($\chi = 1$) and the other a singlet ($\chi = -1$), so $w_{4}\chi$ has antisymmetric form only. Adding, the symmetric parts are $-\tfrac{3}{32} + \tfrac{3}{32} = 0$ times the Georgi-Jarlskog form, plus nothing, so $w_{4}G_{4}$ has no symmetric form, as loc. cit. (iv) states: the $10$ relation with multiple zero. Finally $\tfrac{1}{32} + P_{4} = \tfrac{1}{64}(9(B - L)^{2} - 1)$ is $\tfrac18$ on the lepton values and $0$ on the quark values, which by (iii) weights the $10$ form by $\tfrac18$ on $(L, e^{c})$ and $0$ on $(Q, d^{c})$.

The check builds the module as $32 \times 32$ rational matrices, expands $TT^{\dagger}$ in all $1024$ Majorana monomials by the trace form, reassembles it, splits the degree-four part by support, and confirms (i) to (iv) as operator identities and as mass forms against the stored pairing, including the coefficients $(x, y)$ of (iii) for four even weightings and the quartet traces of every pair monomial of degrees two, four and six.

synthesis.georgi-jarlskog-majorana-momen.technical:
Under Hypothesis (S), project the commutator of the Majorana element $T = v_{1}\cdots v_{5}$ with its adjoint onto the bivectors of the ten (its moment map). The result is one eighth of the thirteenth generator $X = 2T_{3R} - \tfrac32(B - L)$, with pair component $\tfrac18\omega = -\tfrac{3}{16}(B - L)$ and rung component $\tfrac14 T_{3R}$.

Functions of the full moment map, multiplied into the rung vector $w_{4}$, give only the relation of a single $10$, $|y_{e}| = |y_{d}|$. Split along Pati-Salam they give more: $w_{4}\mu_{P}$ is the grade-three ($120$) direction, and $w_{4}\mu_{R}\mu_{P} = \tfrac{3}{256}(T_{\mathrm{GJ}} - w_{4}(B - L))$ has as symmetric part the Georgi-Jarlskog $126$ form, with ratio $3$, and as antisymmetric part the grade-three form, with equal moduli. It acts only on the singlet sectors, the one-sided coupling of Pati-Salam. Clause (i) is the standard relation between the moment map of a weight vector and its weight, here the $\uu(1)_{X}$ of $\mathrm{Spin}(10) \supset SU(5) \times U(1)_{X}$, and is transport-absent; after it $T$ plays no further role, and (iv) is the identity $w_{4}T_{3R}(B - L) = -\tfrac14\bigl(T_{\mathrm{GJ}} - w_{4}(B - L)\bigr)$ among $w_{4}$, $T_{3R}$ and $B - L$. The series' missing factor is therefore the pair component of the moment map of an element it derives. A coupling constant, and a reason for the dynamics to take this composite, are not derived.
synthesis.georgi-jarlskog-majorana-momen.lay: The series could not produce the term that makes the muon about three times heavier than the strange quark at high energy: it had the three ingredients but no way to multiply them together. This result shows that, under the series' slot-statistics hypothesis (S), one of those ingredients, the charge that distinguishes quarks from leptons, is exactly what the series' own heavy-neutrino element produces when it is squared and projected onto the symmetries of the Pati-Salam picture. Multiplying the Higgs direction by the quark-lepton piece alone gives only a pattern that couples different families; multiplying it by both of the element's Pati-Salam pieces gives the Georgi-Jarlskog factor of three, together with that pattern. What is still missing is the strength of this coupling, which nothing in the series fixes.

proofs.main:
Work on the module $\Lambda^{\bullet}(W \oplus R_{2})$ with the occupation basis; the species of the sixteen are those Hypothesis (S) names, through Proposition \claimref{standard-model.under-s-composites-state-space-spinor}: by $(N_{W}, N_{R})$, $e^{c} = (0, 2)$, $Q = (1, 1)$, $u^{c} = (2, 0)$, $d^{c} = (2, 2)$, $L = (3, 1)$, $\nu^{c} = (0, 0)$. Write $s_{i} = v_{i} \wedge w_{i} = n_{i} - \tfrac12$, so that $\omega = s_{1} + s_{2} + s_{3}$, $B - L = 1 - \tfrac23 N_{W} = -\tfrac23\,\omega$ and $T_{3R} = \tfrac12(N_{R} - 1) = \tfrac12(s_{4} + s_{5})$.

(i) $TT^{\dagger}$ is the projector onto the full state and $T^{\dagger}T$ the projector onto the empty state, so $[T, T^{\dagger}] = P_{12345} - P_{\emptyset}$ is diagonal in the occupation basis. In the orthonormal Majorana basis $a_{i} = v_{i} + w_{i}$, $b_{i} = v_{i} - w_{i}$ ($a_{i}^{2} = 1$, $b_{i}^{2} = -1$) the bivectors are trace-orthogonal, and the coefficient of $e_{x}e_{y}$ in the projection of a matrix $M$ is $\mathrm{tr}((e_{x}e_{y})^{-1}M)/32$. A diagonal matrix has trace zero against every bivector that changes some occupation, which leaves only $a_{i}b_{i} = -2s_{i}$; and $\mathrm{tr}(s_{i}(P_{12345} - P_{\emptyset})) = \tfrac12 - (-\tfrac12) = 1$ while $\mathrm{tr}(s_{i}^{2}) = 8$. Hence $\mu(T) = \sum_{i}\tfrac18 s_{i}$, with no mixed pair-rung component. Splitting the sum gives $\mu_{P} = \tfrac18\omega = -\tfrac{3}{16}(B - L)$ and $\mu_{R} = \tfrac18(s_{4} + s_{5}) = \tfrac14 T_{3R}$, and $\tfrac18 X = \tfrac14 T_{3R} - \tfrac{3}{16}(B - L)$ is the same element; $X$ is the thirteenth generator in the form Proposition \claimref{standard-model.majorana-element} records. The split is the one Proposition \claimref{standard-model.automorphisms-preserve-slot-pair-split-are} selects: the automorphisms preserving the slot/pair split are Pati-Salam, whose Lie algebra is $\so(6) \oplus \so(4)$ on the pair and rung bivectors.

(ii) $\mu(T) = \tfrac18(N - \tfrac52)$ with $N$ the total occupation, so $p(\mu(T))$ acts on each occupation state by a scalar depending only on $N$. On the sixteen the Yukawa pairs have $N(e^{c}) = N(Q) = 2$ and $N(L) = N(d^{c}) = 4$. With $\beta$ the symmetric form of $w_{4}$ (the $10$, Proposition \claimref{families.doublet-direction-module-georgi-jarlskog-clebsch}), $B(L, w_{4}p\,e^{c}) = p_{2}\beta(L, e^{c})$, $B(e^{c}, w_{4}p\,L) = p_{4}\beta(e^{c}, L)$, $B(Q, w_{4}p\,d^{c}) = p_{4}\beta(Q, d^{c})$ and $B(d^{c}, w_{4}p\,Q) = p_{2}\beta(d^{c}, Q)$, where $p_{k}$ is the value at $N = k$. The symmetric part is $\tfrac12(p_{2} + p_{4})\beta$ on both pairs, a multiple of the $10$ form.

(iii) $w_{4}\mu_{P} = \tfrac18 w_{4}\omega = -\tfrac{3}{16}w_{4}(B - L)$, which Proposition \claimref{standard-model.grade-three-georgi-jarlskog-direction} shows to be pure grade three with antisymmetric form.

(iv) $w_{4}s_{4} = w_{4}(n_{4} - \tfrac12) = \tfrac12 w_{4}$, since $w_{4}n_{4} = w_{4}$. So $w_{4}\mu_{R}\mu_{P} = \tfrac{1}{64}w_{4}(s_{4} + s_{5})\omega = \tfrac{1}{64}\bigl(\tfrac12 w_{4}\omega + w_{4}s_{5}\omega\bigr)$. By Proposition \claimref{families.doublet-direction-module-georgi-jarlskog-clebsch}(i), $T_{\mathrm{GJ}} = \tfrac43 w_{4}s_{5}\omega$, so the composite is $\tfrac{1}{64}\bigl(\tfrac34 T_{\mathrm{GJ}} - \tfrac34 w_{4}(B - L)\bigr) = \tfrac{3}{256}\bigl(T_{\mathrm{GJ}} - w_{4}(B - L)\bigr) = \tfrac{3}{256}w_{4}(B - L)(\chi - 1)$. $T_{\mathrm{GJ}}$ has symmetric form with ratio $3$ (that proposition, (ii)) and $w_{4}(B - L)$ antisymmetric form (Proposition \claimref{standard-model.grade-three-georgi-jarlskog-direction}); their entries on $(L, e^{c})$ and $(Q, d^{c})$ have equal moduli, $1$ and $\tfrac13$. Since $\chi - 1 = -2$ on $N_{R}$ even and $0$ on $N_{R} = 1$, the composite annihilates the doublet sector.

The script builds the module as exact integer matrices with the pairing of Lemma \claimref{standard-model.invariant-pairing-five-modes}, checks the pairing's $\so(10)$ invariance on sample bivectors, reproduces the forms of $w_{4}$, $T_{\mathrm{GJ}}$ and $w_{4}(B - L)$ that the cited propositions state, computes the projection in (i) over all forty-five bivectors and checks $[\mu(T), T] = \tfrac58 T$, verifies (ii) for $p = \mu^{k}$, $k \le 5$, and verifies (iii) and (iv) as operator identities and entry by entry on the sixteen.

synthesis.georgi-jarlskog-square-of-majo.technical:
Under Hypothesis (S) the square $TT^{\dagger}$ of the Majorana element is the projector onto the fully occupied state, the product of the five occupation numbers. Expanded in the Clifford monomials of the ten Majorana generators it has a scalar part $\tfrac{1}{32}$, a bivector part equal to half the moment map, and a degree-four part $4\mu^{2} - \tfrac{5}{64}$, a polynomial in the moment map that, multiplied into the rung vector, gives no symmetric mass form at all (the relation of a single $10$ with multiple zero): it takes opposite values on the two states of each pair the rung vector couples.

Split along Pati-Salam, the degree-four part has a piece built from both the pair and the rung modes, and that piece is exactly $8\mu_{R}\mu_{P}$, an $\su(2)_{L}$ singlet in the $(15,1,3)$. The rung vector times it is $\tfrac{3}{32}(T_{\mathrm{GJ}} - w_{4}(B - L))$: the Georgi-Jarlskog $126$ form with ratio $3$ plus the grade-three form with equal moduli, the composite of the stored moment-map result. That composite was written as a product of two moment-map components, quartic in $T$; this shows the same operator is also the $(15,1,3)$ part of $TT^{\dagger}$, so it already appears at second order in a vev along $T$. Read that way, a vev $c$ along $T$ gives the right-handed Majorana mass at first order and the Georgi-Jarlskog term at second order, $|c|^{2}$; which polynomial is the physical composite is a reading, not derived. The coefficient of the Pati-Salam split, and so the size of the $126$ relative to the $10$, is not determined. If the vev carries an $S_{3}$-invariant family matrix, the term is family-blind on the light plane and does not by itself single out the second family.
synthesis.georgi-jarlskog-square-of-majo.lay: Under the framework's slot hypothesis (S), the element that gives the right-handed neutrino its large mass also, when squared, contains the ingredient behind the factor of three between the muon and strange-quark masses at high energy. An earlier result found that ingredient as a product of four copies of this element; here it appears already in the square, the piece of the square that mixes the quark-lepton charge with the right-handed weak charge. So, read this way, if this element acquires a value that breaks the symmetry, the neutrino mass appears in proportion to that value and the factor-of-three term already in proportion to its square. On its own the term does not pick out the second family of particles. How large the factor-of-three term is compared with the ordinary mass term is still not fixed.

proofs.main:
Work on the module $\Lambda^{\bullet}(W \oplus R_{2})$ of Proposition \claimref{synthesis.georgi-jarlskog-majorana-moment-map}, with $\beta_{i} = v_{i}\wedge w_{i} = n_{i} - \tfrac12$, so that $\mu = \tfrac18\sum_{i \le 5}\beta_{i}$, $\mu_{P} = \tfrac18(\beta_{1} + \beta_{2} + \beta_{3}) = \tfrac18\omega$ and $\mu_{R} = \tfrac18(\beta_{4} + \beta_{5})$ (clause (i) of that proposition). In terms of the Majorana generators, $a_{i}b_{i} = (v_{i} + w_{i})(v_{i} - w_{i}) = w_{i}v_{i} - v_{i}w_{i} = -2\beta_{i}$, a monomial of degree two, and for $i \ne l$ the product $\beta_{i}\beta_{l}$ is a monomial of degree four.

(i) $T^{\dagger} = w_{5}w_{4}w_{3}w_{2}w_{1}$, and since $v_{i}w_{i}$ commutes with $v_{l}$ and $w_{l}$ for $l \ne i$, $TT^{\dagger} = \prod_{i}v_{i}w_{i} = \prod_{i}n_{i}$, the projector onto the full state (the Majorana element raises the empty state $\nu^{c}$ to the full state, Proposition \claimref{standard-model.majorana-element}(1)). With $n_{i} = \tfrac12 + \beta_{i}$ and the $\beta_{i}$ commuting, $\prod_{i}(\tfrac12 + \beta_{i}) = \sum_{S}2^{-(5 - |S|)}\prod_{i \in S}\beta_{i}$, and $\prod_{i \in S}\beta_{i}$ is a single monomial of degree $2|S|$. The degree-zero part is $2^{-5} = \tfrac{1}{32}$, the degree-two part $\tfrac{1}{16}\sum_{i}\beta_{i} = \tfrac12\mu$, and the degree-four part $G_{4} = \tfrac18 e_{2}(\beta)$ with $e_{2}$ the second elementary symmetric polynomial. Since $\beta_{i}^{2} = \tfrac14$, $e_{2}(\beta) = \tfrac12\bigl((\sum\beta_{i})^{2} - \tfrac54\bigr) = \tfrac12(64\mu^{2} - \tfrac54)$, so $G_{4} = 4\mu^{2} - \tfrac{5}{64}$.

(ii) The monomials of $G_{4}$ are $\beta_{i}\beta_{l}$, $i < l$; those with one index among the pairs and one among the rungs sum to $X_{4} = \tfrac18(\beta_{1} + \beta_{2} + \beta_{3})(\beta_{4} + \beta_{5}) = \tfrac18(8\mu_{P})(8\mu_{R}) = 8\mu_{R}\mu_{P}$ (the factors commute). $\beta_{4} + \beta_{5} = N_{R} - 1 = 2T_{3R}$ commutes with the $\su(2)_{L}$ generators $v_{4}w_{5}$, $v_{5}w_{4}$, $n_{4} - n_{5}$ (they preserve $N_{R}$) and fails to commute with $v_{4}v_{5}$, which raises $N_{R}$ by two; $\omega$ commutes with everything diagonal. The pair-rung monomials of degree four span $\Lambda^{2}$ of the pair space tensored with $\Lambda^{2}$ of the rung space, which under $\su(4) \oplus \su(2)_{L} \oplus \su(2)_{R}$ is $(15,3,1) \oplus (15,1,3)$ (the bivectors of the six-dimensional pair space form the adjoint $15$, those of the four-dimensional rung space $(3,1) \oplus (1,3)$; standard), and an $\su(2)_{L}$ singlet lies in $(15,1,3)$.

(iii) By Proposition \claimref{synthesis.georgi-jarlskog-majorana-moment-map}(iv), $w_{4}\mu_{R}\mu_{P} = \tfrac{3}{256}(T_{\mathrm{GJ}} - w_{4}(B - L))$, so $w_{4}X_{4} = 8 \cdot \tfrac{3}{256}(\cdots) = \tfrac{3}{32}(T_{\mathrm{GJ}} - w_{4}(B - L))$; the mass forms $B(\psi, w_{4}X_{4}\varphi)$, with the pairing $B$ of Lemma \claimref{standard-model.invariant-pairing-five-modes}, follow from that proposition's (iv), scaled by $8$, with $T_{\mathrm{GJ}}$ and the ratio $3$ from Proposition \claimref{families.doublet-direction-module-georgi-jarlskog-clebsch}.

(iv) $G_{4}$ is a polynomial in $\mu$, so by Proposition \claimref{synthesis.georgi-jarlskog-majorana-moment-map}(ii) the symmetric part of the mass form of $w_{4}G_{4}$ is a multiple of the $10$ form; the multiple is zero. Indeed $\mu = \tfrac18(N - \tfrac52)$ with $N$ the total mode number, so $G_{4} = 4\mu^{2} - \tfrac{5}{64}$ is diagonal in the occupation basis and equals $\tfrac{5}{16}$, $-\tfrac{1}{16}$, $\tfrac{1}{16}$ on the states of the sixteen with $N = 0, 2, 4$. The pairing of Lemma \claimref{standard-model.invariant-pairing-five-modes} pairs a state with its complement, so $B(\psi, w_{4}\varphi) \ne 0$ on the sixteen needs $N(\psi) + N(\varphi) - 1 = 5$: one state has $N = 2$ and the other $N = 4$. The $10$ form $B(\psi, w_{4}\varphi)$ is symmetric on the sixteen, so the symmetric part of $B(\psi, w_{4}G_{4}\varphi)$ on such a pair is $\tfrac12\bigl(G_{4}(\psi) + G_{4}(\varphi)\bigr)B(\psi, w_{4}\varphi) = \tfrac12(-\tfrac{1}{16} + \tfrac{1}{16})B(\psi, w_{4}\varphi) = 0$.

(v) $(cT)(cT)^{\dagger} = |c|^{2}TT^{\dagger}$, and the expansion is linear, so $X_{4} \mapsto |c|^{2}X_{4}$; the moment map is quadratic, $\mu(cT) = |c|^{2}\mu(T)$, so the product of its two components scales as $|c|^{4}$. The Majorana entry $B(\nu^{c}, cT\nu^{c})$ is linear in $c$. At $|c| = 1$ the operators $X_{4}(T)$ and $8\mu_{R}(T)\mu_{P}(T)$ coincide; what (v) shows is that this operator occurs at second order in a vev along $T$, not only at fourth; which of the two is the physical composite is a reading.

The check builds the module as $32 \times 32$ rational matrices, expands $TT^{\dagger}$ in all $1024$ Majorana monomials by the trace form (each monomial a signed permutation, cross-checked against matrix products and its inverse), reassembles it, and confirms (i) to (v), including the mass forms of (iii) and (iv) against the pairing, and the scaling with $c = 3$.

synthesis.georgi-jarlskog-weight-free-on.technical:
The open number of the problem, the weight of the $(15,1,1)$ part of the Majorana square against the rung vector's $10$ term, is shown to be unconstrained by every relation the store holds. First, a coupling through functions of the Majorana element itself cannot produce it: $T$ and $T^{\dagger}$ generate a five-dimensional algebra, and the down-type rung vector times any element of it gives a multiple of the $10$ form, so the Georgi-Jarlskog form appears only after projecting the square on a Pati-Salam component. Second, the weight $b/a$ of that projection sets the lepton-to-quark ratio of the down-type form as $(32a + 3b)/(32a - b)$, and on each family it is exactly the Clebsch structure's $w_{d}f$ against $v_{d}Y$.

Third, scaling the $126$'s down-type doublet admixture $w_{d}$ alone leaves the up and neutrino Dirac mass matrices, the Majorana matrix, the light neutrino matrix, Premise (EW), the Majorana scale premise, the neutrino Dirac mass matrix under (EW) and with it Hypothesis (U) in its eigenvalue readings (with $m_{b}/m_{t}$ given; models satisfy the top reading), the chain and the family symmetries unchanged, and multiplies the symmetric part of $M_{d} - M_{e}$ by the same factor. The stored Majorana scaling moves $w_{u}$ and $w_{d}$ together against $f$ and so fixes $w_{d}f$; this one moves $w_{d}$ alone. Exact models with the same up, neutrino and Majorana sectors have second-family factors $3$, $2$ and $\tfrac{37}{19}$, the last at the same bottom mass. So the factor $3$ is not derived: it is read from the measured masses. The check verifies all four clauses exactly, on the $32$-dimensional module and on two family-matrix models (one diagonal, one with off-diagonal entries and a $120$) for four values of $\mu$.
synthesis.georgi-jarlskog-weight-free-on.lay: In the version of the theory where quarks and leptons are unified, the mass of the strange quark and of the muon come from two kinds of Higgs field: one gives them equal masses, the other gives the muon three times the strange quark's mass, which is what the measurements suggest at very high energies. How much of each kind enters is a number. This result shows that nothing the theory has stored fixes that number. A coupling built from the theory's heavy-neutrino element alone gives only the equal-mass kind. Changing the weight of the second kind, through one unmeasured Higgs mixing, leaves every stored relation true, including the assumptions about the heavy neutrino and the top quark. Only the masses of the down-type quarks and the charged leptons change. So the factor three is taken from the data, not predicted.

synthesis.imported-atlas-charged-higgs-t.formal: The ATLAS search for charged Higgs bosons $H^{\pm}$ produced in top-quark decays $t \to bH^{+}$ or in association with a top quark, and decaying as $H^{\pm} \to \tau^{\pm}\nu_{\tau}$, with $140$ fb$^{-1}$ of proton-proton collisions at $\sqrt{s} = 13$ TeV, covering $80 \le m_{H^{\pm}} \le 3000$ GeV, finds no significant excess over the Standard Model expectation and sets $95$ per cent confidence upper limits on the production cross-section times branching fraction from $4.5$ pb to $0.4$ fb over that range. In the range $80 \le m_{H^{\pm}} \le 160$ GeV, with the Standard Model $t\bar{t}$ cross-section assumed, these are upper limits on $\mathcal{B}(t \to bH^{+}) \times \mathcal{B}(H^{+} \to \tau\nu)$ with values between $0.27\%$ and $0.02\%$. \emph{Provenance:} \cite{ATLAS2025ChargedHiggsTauNu} (abstract).
synthesis.imported-atlas-charged-higgs-t.technical: ATLAS searched the full data set of the LHC's second run for an electrically charged scalar that is lighter than the top quark and is produced in its decays, or heavier and produced alongside it, decaying to a tau lepton and a neutrino. Nothing beyond the Standard Model was seen. For charged-scalar masses between $80$ and $160$ GeV the result bounds the fraction of top quarks that decay to a bottom quark and the charged scalar, times the scalar's branching to a tau and a neutrino, below values between a quarter of a per cent and two hundredths of a per cent across that mass range.
synthesis.imported-atlas-charged-higgs-t.lay: If a heavy electrically charged cousin of the Higgs particle existed and were lighter than the top quark, top quarks would sometimes decay into it. The ATLAS experiment at CERN looked for this in its full 2015 to 2018 data and found nothing: at most a few top quarks in a thousand, and in part of the mass range a few in ten thousand, can decay that way when the charged particle then decays to a tau lepton.

imported_from.citation: ATLAS Collaboration, Search for charged Higgs bosons produced in top-quark decays or in association with top quarks and decaying via $H^{\pm} \to \tau^{\pm}\nu_{\tau}$ in $13$ TeV $pp$ collisions with the ATLAS detector, Phys. Rev. D 111 (2025), 072006; arXiv:2412.17584.

synthesis.imported-b-meson-mixing-inputs.formal:
\begin{enumerate}
\item[(i)] \emph{(Operators and vacuum insertion.)} For a neutral meson $M = (q\bar{q}')$, with colour indices $\alpha$, $\beta$, the $\Delta F = 2$ operators include $Q_{2} = \bar{q}^{\alpha}_{R}q'^{\alpha}_{L}\,\bar{q}^{\beta}_{R}q'^{\beta}_{L}$ and $Q_{4} = \bar{q}^{\alpha}_{R}q'^{\alpha}_{L}\,\bar{q}^{\beta}_{L}q'^{\beta}_{R}$, with $\tilde{Q}_{2}$ obtained by $L \leftrightarrow R$; in the vacuum-insertion approximation, with the bag parameters restored and relativistic normalisation, $\langle\bar{M}|Q_{2}|M\rangle = -\tfrac{5}{24}R\,m_{M}f_{M}^{2}B_{2}$ and $\langle\bar{M}|Q_{4}|M\rangle = (\tfrac{1}{24} + \tfrac14R)\,m_{M}f_{M}^{2}B_{4}$, $R = (m_{M}/(m_{q} + m_{q'}))^{2}$ \cite[Eqs.~(3), (8)]{Gabbiani1996}.
\item[(ii)] \emph{(Decay constants, $N_{f} = 2 + 1 + 1$.)} $f_{B} = 190.0(1.3)$ MeV, $f_{B_{s}} = 230.3(1.3)$ MeV, $f_{K^{\pm}} = 155.7(3)$ MeV \cite{FLAG2024}.
\item[(iii)] \emph{(Bag parameters, $\overline{\mathrm{MS}}$ at $\mu = m_{b}$.)} For $B_{s}$, $B_{2} = 0.817(43)$, $B_{4} = 1.033(47)$; for $B_{d}$, $B_{2} = 0.769(44)$, $B_{4} = 1.077(55)$ \cite[Table VI]{HPQCD2019}.
\item[(iv)] \emph{(Mass differences.)} $\Delta m_{s} = 17.765 \pm 0.006$ ps$^{-1}$ and $\Delta m_{d} = 0.5069 \pm 0.0019$ ps$^{-1}$ \cite{PDG2025}.
\item[(v)] \emph{(Quark mixing without $B$ mixing.)} From tree-level processes: $|V_{cb}| = (41.1 \pm 1.2) \times 10^{-3}$ (semileptonic $b \to c$, inclusive and exclusive average), $|V_{ub}| = (3.82 \pm 0.20) \times 10^{-3}$, $\gamma = (65.7 \pm 3.0)^{\circ}$, the tree-level kaon-decay determination of $|V_{us}|$, $0.22431 \pm 0.00085$ (not the global-fit value of the stored quantity, since the global fit uses $B$ mixing), $|V_{cd}| = 0.221 \pm 0.004$, $|V_{cs}| = 0.975 \pm 0.006$, $|V_{tb}| = 1.010 \pm 0.027$ \cite{PDG2025}. The direct values $|V_{ts}| = (41.5 \pm 0.9) \times 10^{-3}$ and $|V_{td}| = (8.6 \pm 0.2) \times 10^{-3}$ are extracted from $\Delta m_{s}$ and $\Delta m_{d}$ with lattice inputs, so they are valid only when mixing has no other tree-level contribution. Three-family unitarity fixes $|V_{ts}|$ and $|V_{td}|$ from the tree-level moduli and $\gamma$: $|V_{ts}| = |V_{cb}|(1 + O(\lambda^{2}))$ and $|V_{td}| = \lambda|V_{cb}|(1 - 2R_{u}\cos\gamma + R_{u}^{2})^{1/2}(1 + O(\lambda^{2}))$, $\lambda = |V_{us}|$, $R_{u} = |V_{ub}|/(\lambda|V_{cb}|)(1 + O(\lambda^{2}))$.
\end{enumerate}
synthesis.imported-b-meson-mixing-inputs.technical: These are the inputs any tree-level bound on neutral-meson mixing from a new scalar needs. The scalar's exchange produces the left-right operators $Q_{2}$ and $Q_{4}$; their matrix elements between a meson and its antiparticle are the vacuum-insertion forms of Gabbiani and collaborators corrected by lattice bag parameters, with the decay constants from the FLAG averages and the bag parameters from HPQCD. The measured mass differences are the Particle Data Group averages. Quark mixing must not be taken from the $B$-mixing extractions when a new tree-level contribution is under test; the tree-level determinations of $|V_{cb}|$, $|V_{ub}|$ and the angle $\gamma$, with unitarity of the three-family matrix, fix $|V_{ts}|$ and $|V_{td}|$ independently.
synthesis.imported-b-meson-mixing-inputs.lay: Mesons made of a bottom quark and a lighter antiquark turn into their own antiparticles and back at rates measured to a fraction of a percent. To test whether a new particle would speed this up, one needs how strongly the quarks are bound in the meson, taken from large lattice computations, the measured rates, and how the quark types mix, taken from decays that the new particle would not affect. The series takes all of these from the standard compilations.

synthesis.imported-coleman-weinberg-gild.formal:
(i) \emph{(Radiative breaking.)} In a gauge theory whose tree potential has no mass term, one-loop corrections can produce a minimum away from the origin, so that the symmetry is broken spontaneously and a mass scale appears through the running of a dimensionless coupling (dimensional transmutation) \cite{ColemanWeinberg1973}.

(ii) \emph{(The scalon.)} Let the tree potential $V_{0}(\varphi) = \lambda_{ijkl}\varphi_{i}\varphi_{j}\varphi_{k}\varphi_{l}$ of real scalars be scale free, and let it have a flat direction: a unit vector $n$ with $V_{0}(n) = 0$ at a minimum of $V_{0}$ on the unit sphere. Along $\varphi = \rho n$ the one-loop potential is $A\rho^{4} + B\rho^{4}\ln(\rho^{2}/\mu^{2})$ with
\[
B = \frac{1}{64\pi^{2}v^{4}}\Bigl(3\sum_{\text{vectors}}M_{V}^{4} + \sum_{\text{real scalars}}M_{S}^{4} - 4\sum_{\text{Dirac fermions}}M_{F}^{4}\Bigr),
\]
the masses being the tree masses at $\rho = v = \langle\rho\rangle$ (each colour counted), and the one scalar along the flat direction (the scalon, the pseudo-Goldstone boson of broken scale invariance) has mass $m_{S}^{2} = 8Bv^{2}$:
\[
8\pi^{2}v^{2}m_{S}^{2} = 3\sum_{\text{vectors}}M_{V}^{4} + \sum_{\text{real scalars}}M_{S}^{4} - 4\sum_{\text{Dirac fermions}}M_{F}^{4},
\]
positive exactly when the bosons outweigh the fermions. \emph{Provenance:} \cite{GildenerWeinberg1976}; the displayed form as in \cite{FootKobakhidzeVolkas2007}, equations (10) to (14).
synthesis.imported-coleman-weinberg-gild.technical: Coleman and Weinberg showed that a theory with no mass parameter at all can still break its symmetry, the scale being generated by quantum corrections and the running of a coupling. Gildener and Weinberg extended this to many scalars: if the tree-level potential, built only from quartic terms, has a flat direction along which it vanishes, the one-loop correction picks a point on that direction and the scalar along it, the scalon, gets a mass from the fourth powers of every mass the vacuum generates, with weight $3$ for each massive vector, $1$ for each real scalar and $-4$ for each Dirac fermion (per colour). Fermions push the scalon mass down; heavy bosons push it up.
synthesis.imported-coleman-weinberg-gild.lay: Some theories contain no built-in mass scale, yet produce one through quantum effects, as the strong force does for the proton. Coleman and Weinberg found how this can work for a Higgs-like field, and Gildener and Weinberg found the formula for the mass of the resulting light scalar particle: it is set by the masses of all the other particles, with heavy force carriers raising it and heavy quarks lowering it.

imported_from.citation: S. Coleman and E. Weinberg, Radiative corrections as the origin of spontaneous symmetry breaking, Phys. Rev. D 7 (1973), 1888--1910.
E. Gildener and S. Weinberg, Symmetry breaking and scalar bosons, Phys. Rev. D 13 (1976), 3333.
R. Foot, A. Kobakhidze and R. R. Volkas, Electroweak Higgs as a pseudo-Goldstone boson of broken scale invariance, arXiv:0704.1165, equations (10) to (14).

synthesis.imported-fayet-iliopoulos-leve.formal: Let a compact gauge algebra $\mathfrak{g}$ act on a scalar field space with moment maps $\mu_{a}$, so that the D-term potential is $V_{D} = \tfrac12\sum_{a}g_{a}^{2}\mu_{a}^{2}$. A Fayet-Iliopoulos term, a level $\zeta$ shifting the moment maps as $V_{D} = \tfrac12\sum_{a}g_{a}^{2}(\mu_{a} - \zeta_{a})^{2}$ (equivalently a term linear in the auxiliary fields $D^{a}$, $\xi V$ in the vector superfield), is gauge invariant (and, in a supersymmetric theory, supersymmetric) exactly when $\zeta_{a}\mu_{a}$ is invariant, that is when $\zeta$ is fixed by the adjoint action, i.e. lies in the centre of $\mathfrak{g}$. Hence a D-term level exists only for the abelian $\mathfrak{u}(1)$ factors of the gauge algebra and vanishes on every simple factor. \emph{Provenance:} \cite{FayetIliopoulos1974}; the statement as in \cite{ShadmiShirman1999}, Section II.C.2.
synthesis.imported-fayet-iliopoulos-leve.technical: In a gauge theory whose scalar potential is built from the gauge moment maps (the D-terms, as in supersymmetric theories), one may add a constant to a moment map, which shifts where the potential is minimised. Such a constant is allowed only if it is unchanged by the gauge transformations, and the moment maps of a non-abelian factor rotate into each other, so the constant must vanish there; only for an abelian factor, whose moment map is gauge invariant, can it be nonzero. This is the Fayet-Iliopoulos term.
synthesis.imported-fayet-iliopoulos-leve.lay: In some theories of particle forces the energy of the Higgs-like fields can be shifted by a fixed constant, which then decides where the fields settle. Fayet and Iliopoulos introduced this constant; it is allowed only for the simplest, electromagnetism-like kind of force, not for the forces whose charges rotate into one another.

imported_from.citation: P. Fayet and J. Iliopoulos, Spontaneously broken supergauge symmetries and Goldstone spinors, Phys. Lett. B 51 (1974), 461--464.
Y. Shadmi and Y. Shirman, Dynamical supersymmetry breaking, arXiv:hep-th/9907225, Section II.C.2, equation (14).

synthesis.imported-general-quartic-runni.technical: The running of quartic scalar couplings in any renormalisable gauge theory is known in closed form: at one loop it is a sum of a quadratic term in the quartics, an anomalous-dimension term from gauge and Yukawa couplings, a Yukawa box and a gauge box; at two loops the terms with quartics alone are a cubic term and a product of the one-loop scalar anomalous dimension with the quartic. Specialised to two Higgs doublets with a discrete symmetry and the type-II assignment of the top and bottom couplings, these give the standard one-loop equations for the five quartics, in which the gauge couplings and the top and bottom couplings enter as stated.
synthesis.imported-general-quartic-runni.lay: How strongly the Higgs-type fields push on one another changes with the energy at which they are probed, by an amount that can be calculated once and for all for any theory of this kind. The general formulas, and their standard form for a theory with two Higgs fields, are taken from the literature; the series uses them to follow its own Higgs field's couplings up in energy.

synthesis.imported-jarlskog-commutator-i.formal:
Numbers, and the entries of the matrices, are read in $\mathrm{span}\{1, I_{4}\}$ (conventions U1; the source writes $i$ for $I_{4}$, $\mathrm{Im}$ is the $I_{4}$-part and $^{*}$ conjugates $I_{4} \mapsto -I_{4}$). Let $H_{u}$, $H_{d}$ be $3 \times 3$ Hermitian matrices with eigenvalues $m_{u}^{2} < m_{c}^{2} < m_{t}^{2}$ and $m_{d}^{2} < m_{s}^{2} < m_{b}^{2}$, $H_{q} = U_{q}\,\mathrm{diag}(\cdot)\,U_{q}^{\dagger}$ with $U_{q}$ unitary, and $V = U_{u}^{\dagger}U_{d}$ (rows $u, c, t$, columns $d, s, b$). Let $J$ be defined by $\mathrm{Im}[V_{ij}V_{kl}V_{il}^{*}V_{kj}^{*}] = J\sum_{m,n}\epsilon_{ikm}\epsilon_{jln}$, so that $J = \mathrm{Im}(V_{us}V_{cb}V_{ub}^{*}V_{cs}^{*})$; it does not depend on the phases of the columns of $U_{u}$ and $U_{d}$. Then
\[
\det[H_{u}, H_{d}] = 2I_{4}J\,F_{u}F_{d},\qquad F_{u} = (m_{t}^{2} - m_{c}^{2})(m_{t}^{2} - m_{u}^{2})(m_{c}^{2} - m_{u}^{2}),\quad F_{d} = (m_{b}^{2} - m_{s}^{2})(m_{b}^{2} - m_{d}^{2})(m_{s}^{2} - m_{d}^{2}).
\]
In particular, with nondegenerate masses in each sector, $J = 0$ if and only if $\det[H_{u}, H_{d}] = 0$; a common eigenvector of $H_{u}$ and $H_{d}$ gives $\det[H_{u}, H_{d}] = 0$ and so $J = 0$. \emph{Provenance:} \cite{Jarlskog1985}; the definition of $J$ as in \cite{PDG2024}.
synthesis.imported-jarlskog-commutator-i.technical: Quark mixing violates the symmetry between matter and antimatter through one number, the Jarlskog invariant $J$, read from the mixing matrix as the imaginary part of a product of four of its entries. Jarlskog showed that it can be read from the mass matrices directly, without diagonalising them: the determinant of the commutator of the up-type and down-type mass squares equals $2I_{4}J$ times the product of all six mass-squared differences within the two sectors. So, when no two masses in a sector are equal, CP violation in quark mixing is absent exactly when that determinant vanishes, and in particular whenever the two mass squares share an eigenvector.
synthesis.imported-jarlskog-commutator-i.lay: The way quarks of different families mix carries one number that measures how much nature distinguishes matter from antimatter in this sector. This standard identity shows that the number can be computed straight from the quark mass matrices, from how far the up-type and down-type matrices fail to commute. If they share even one common direction, the number is zero.

imported_from.citation: C. Jarlskog, Commutator of the quark mass matrices in the standard electroweak model and a measure of maximal CP nonconservation, Phys. Rev. Lett. 55 (1985), 1039--1042.
S. Navas et al. (Particle Data Group), Review of Particle Physics, Phys. Rev. D 110 (2024) 030001.

synthesis.imported-left-right-bidoublet-.formal:
In the left-right symmetric model with gauge group $SU(2)_{L} \times SU(2)_{R} \times U(1)_{B - L}$ and a complex bidoublet $\Phi$ in $(2, 2, 0)$, the most general quark Yukawa coupling to the bidoublet is
\[
\mathcal{L}_{Y} = \bar{Q}_{L}\bigl(h\,\Phi + \tilde{h}\,\tilde{\Phi}\bigr)Q_{R} + \text{h.c.}, \qquad \tilde{\Phi} = \varepsilon\Phi^{*}\varepsilon^{\mathsf{T}}, \quad \varepsilon = \begin{pmatrix} 0 & 1 \\ -1 & 0 \end{pmatrix},
\]
with two independent $3 \times 3$ family matrices $h$ and $\tilde{h}$; $\tilde{\Phi}$ transforms under $SU(2)_{L} \times SU(2)_{R}$ as $\Phi$ does. Numbers, and the entries of the fields and matrices, are read in $\mathrm{span}\{1, I_4\}$ (conventions U1; the source writes $i$ for $I_4$), and $\Phi^{*}$ conjugates the entries, $I_4 \mapsto -I_4$; the source's $\tau_{2}\Phi^{*}\tau_{2}$ is $\varepsilon\Phi^{*}\varepsilon^{\mathsf{T}}$, since $\tau_{2} = -I_4\varepsilon$. With $\langle\Phi\rangle = \operatorname{diag}(\kappa, \kappa'e^{I_4\theta})$, $\kappa$, $\kappa'$, $\theta$ real ($\theta$ is the phase the cited form calls $\alpha$), the quark mass matrices are
\[
M_{U} = \kappa h + \kappa'e^{-I_4\theta}\tilde{h}, \qquad M_{D} = \kappa'e^{I_4\theta}h + \kappa\tilde{h}.
\]
\emph{Provenance:} \cite{SenjanovicMohapatra1975}; the displayed form as in \cite{ZhangAnJiMohapatra2008}, equations (7), (12), (13).

\emph{Reading in the series' chart (identification of formulas, not part of the import).} With the rung-$4$ components of the rung field read as $\alpha \leftrightarrow \kappa$, $\beta \leftrightarrow \kappa'e^{I_{4}\theta}$ (the unit $I_{4}$ acting as the field theory's unit on rung values), $Y \leftrightarrow h$ and $\tilde{Y} \leftrightarrow \tilde{h}$, these are the mass matrices $M_{u} = \alpha Y + \bar{\beta}\tilde{Y}$, $M_{d} = \beta Y + \bar{\alpha}\tilde{Y}$ of the coupling $Yc + \tilde{Y}c^{*}$ of the rung field and its conjugate.
synthesis.imported-left-right-bidoublet-.technical: In the left-right symmetric extension of the Standard Model the Higgs field that gives the quarks their masses is a bidoublet, a doublet of both the left-handed and the right-handed weak isospin. It and its conjugate transform alike, so the quarks can couple to each with its own family matrix. The two vacuum values of the bidoublet then mix the two matrices, one combination giving the up-type masses and the other the down-type masses; with one matrix only, the up-type and down-type mass matrices would be proportional.
synthesis.imported-left-right-bidoublet-.lay: In left-right symmetric theories, which treat left-handed and right-handed particles alike at high energies, the Higgs field and its mirror image can each couple to the quarks with their own strengths. The up-type and down-type quark masses then come from different mixtures of the two couplings, which is how such theories let the top quark be much heavier than the bottom quark.

imported_from.citation: G. Senjanovic and R. N. Mohapatra, Exact left-right symmetry and spontaneous violation of parity, Phys. Rev. D 12 (1975), 1502.
Y. Zhang, H. An, X. Ji and R. N. Mohapatra, General CP violation in minimal left-right symmetric model and constraints on the right-handed scale, arXiv:0712.4218, equations (7), (12) and (13).

synthesis.imported-long-lived-charged-pa.technical: An electrically charged particle that lives long enough to cross a collider detector leaves a slow, heavily ionising track that the standard searches for heavy stable charged particles pick out. CMS, in the data of the LHC's first run, excluded long-lived staus produced directly in pairs through the electroweak interaction up to $339$ GeV, and up to $500$ GeV when production through heavier states is included; ATLAS, in part of the second run's data, excluded directly pair-produced long-lived staus up to $430$ GeV. A stable charged scalar of comparable electroweak couplings is constrained by the same searches, through a reinterpretation of these limits.
synthesis.imported-long-lived-charged-pa.lay: If a new electrically charged particle were stable, or lived long enough to cross a detector, it would leave an unusual slow and heavily ionising track. The CMS and ATLAS experiments at CERN looked for such tracks and found none, ruling out long-lived partners of the tau lepton lighter than several hundred GeV.

synthesis.imported-mssm-charged-higgs-tr.formal:
In the minimal supersymmetric extension of the Standard Model, whose Higgs sector is two complex doublets with the quartic couplings fixed by the gauge couplings through the D-terms, the tree-level masses of the charged Higgs pair $H^{\pm}$ and of the CP-odd neutral scalar $A$ satisfy
\[
m_{H^{\pm}}^{2} \;=\; m_{A}^{2} + M_{W}^{2},
\]
with $M_{W}$ the tree-level $W$ mass; in particular $m_{H^{\pm}} > M_{W}$ at tree level. Loop corrections modify the relation. \emph{Provenance:} \cite{GunionHaber1986}, \cite{Djouadi2008} (Section 1.2.2), \cite{DudleyKolda2009} (equation (1)).
synthesis.imported-mssm-charged-higgs-tr.technical: In the minimal supersymmetric Standard Model the Higgs potential's quartic terms come from the gauge interactions, so the Higgs masses at tree level are fixed by two parameters, usually the CP-odd mass $m_{A}$ and the ratio of the two vacuum values. The charged pair's mass is then tied to the CP-odd one by $m_{H^{\pm}}^{2} = m_{A}^{2} + M_{W}^{2}$, which places the charged pair above the $W$ mass at tree level. Radiative corrections shift the relation slightly.
synthesis.imported-mssm-charged-higgs-tr.lay: In the simplest supersymmetric version of the Standard Model there are five Higgs particles, and their masses are not independent. At the simplest level of approximation the mass of the electrically charged pair is fixed by the mass of one of the neutral ones and the mass of the W boson.

imported_from.citation: J. F. Gunion and H. E. Haber, Higgs bosons in supersymmetric models (I), Nucl. Phys. B 272 (1986), 1--76.
A. Djouadi, The anatomy of electroweak symmetry breaking. Tome II: The Higgs bosons in the minimal supersymmetric model, Phys. Rept. 459 (2008), 1--241, Section 1.2.2; arXiv:hep-ph/0503173.
B. Dudley and C. Kolda, Constraining the charged Higgs mass in the MSSM: a low-energy approach, arXiv:0901.3337, equation (1).

synthesis.imported-two-doublet-scalon-su.technical: If the Higgs boson is the pseudo-Goldstone boson of broken scale invariance in a model with two Higgs doublets, its mass comes from one loop and is fixed by the fourth powers of the other masses; the extra scalars must then compensate the top quark, which fixes the sum of their fourth powers: about $540$ GeV to the fourth power. Separately, the precision measurements of the $Z$ resonance at LEP and SLC fix the width of its decays into invisible particles, equivalent to $2.984 \pm 0.008$ species of light neutrino, so any additional light neutral particles the $Z$ can decay into are tightly limited.
synthesis.imported-two-doublet-scalon-su.lay: In one class of theories the Higgs boson gets its mass purely from quantum effects, and if the Higgs field comes in two copies the extra particles must be heavy enough to make up for the top quark: a standard calculation puts a combined measure of their masses at about $540$ GeV. Separately, experiments at the Z boson showed there are just three kinds of light neutrino, which leaves no room for further light neutral particles the Z could produce. The series takes both from the literature.

synthesis.imported-two-doublet-top-to-ch.formal:
In a two-Higgs-doublet model with ratio of vacuum values $\tan\beta$, in which the charged Higgs $H^{+}$ couples to $\bar{t}b$ through $m_{t}\cot\beta$ (the top Yukawa term) and $m_{b}\tan\beta$ (type II and flipped), at tree level and with the bottom mass neglected in the kinematics,
\[
\Gamma(t \to W^{+}b) = \frac{G_{F}m_{t}}{8\sqrt{2}\pi}\bigl(m_{t}^{2} + 2M_{W}^{2}\bigr)\Bigl(1 - \frac{M_{W}^{2}}{m_{t}^{2}}\Bigr)^{2}, \qquad
\Gamma(t \to H^{+}b) = \frac{G_{F}m_{t}}{8\sqrt{2}\pi}\bigl(m_{t}^{2}\cot^{2}\beta + m_{b}^{2}\tan^{2}\beta\bigr)\Bigl(1 - \frac{m_{H^{\pm}}^{2}}{m_{t}^{2}}\Bigr)^{2}.
\]
Dropping the $m_{b}^{2}$ term, which in type I carries $\cot^{2}\beta$ as well, the ratio is
\[
\frac{\Gamma(t \to bH^{+})}{\Gamma(t \to bW^{+})} = \cot^{2}\beta\,\frac{(1 - x)^{2}}{(1 - y)^{2}(1 + 2y)}, \qquad x = \frac{m_{H^{\pm}}^{2}}{m_{t}^{2}},\ y = \frac{M_{W}^{2}}{m_{t}^{2}},
\]
for $m_{H^{\pm}} < m_{t}$. \emph{Provenance:} \cite{LoganMacLennan2010} (equations (A1), (A2)).
synthesis.imported-two-doublet-top-to-ch.technical: A top quark decays almost always to a bottom quark and a $W$ boson. If a charged Higgs boson lighter than the top exists, the top can also decay to a bottom quark and the charged Higgs, at a rate set by the charged Higgs's coupling to the top and bottom. In a two-doublet model that coupling is the top's mass coupling times $\cot\beta$ (with a bottom-mass term that is negligible unless $\tan\beta$ is large), so the ratio of the two decay rates is $\cot^{2}\beta$ times a phase-space factor built from the masses of the top, the $W$ and the charged Higgs.
synthesis.imported-two-doublet-top-to-ch.lay: A top quark normally decays into a bottom quark and a W boson. If there were an electrically charged Higgs particle lighter than the top, some top quarks would decay into it instead. How often depends on how strongly the charged Higgs talks to the top and bottom quarks, and this formula gives the ratio of the two decay rates in the standard two-Higgs-field model.

imported_from.citation: H. E. Logan and D. MacLennan, Charged Higgs phenomenology in the flipped two Higgs doublet model, Phys. Rev. D 81 (2010), 075016, Appendix A, equations (A1) and (A2); arXiv:1002.4916.

synthesis.imported-two-loop-yukawa-gauge.technical: In a general gauge theory the Yukawa couplings first affect the running of a gauge coupling at two loops. For a simple gauge group the two-loop beta function contains, besides the purely gauge, fermion and scalar terms, the term $-2\kappa\,g^{3}Y_{4}(F)/(4\pi)^{4}$ with $Y_{4}(F) = \Tr[C_{2}(F)Y^{a}Y^{a\dagger}]/d(G)$, where $\kappa = \tfrac12$ for Weyl fermions; for a product group the same term appears for each factor with that factor's Casimir. These are the general results of Machacek and Vaughn, as restated by Luo, Wang and Xiao.
synthesis.imported-two-loop-yukawa-gauge.lay: The strengths of the forces change with the energy at which they are measured, and the rate of change can be computed order by order. At the second order the couplings of matter particles to the Higgs-like fields begin to contribute. This standard result gives that contribution for any gauge theory. It is taken from the literature.

imported_from.citation: M. E. Machacek and M. T. Vaughn, Two-loop renormalization group equations in a general quantum field theory (I). Wave function renormalization, Nucl. Phys. B 222 (1983), 83--103.
M. E. Machacek and M. T. Vaughn, Two-loop renormalization group equations in a general quantum field theory (II). Yukawa couplings, Nucl. Phys. B 236 (1984), 221--232.
M. Luo, H. Wang and Y. Xiao, Two-loop renormalization group equations in general gauge field theories, Phys. Rev. D 67 (2003), 065019.

synthesis.imported-witten-global-su2-ano.formal: In four dimensions, an $SU(2)$ gauge theory whose fermions are an odd number of left-handed Weyl doublets, and no other representations, is mathematically inconsistent: since $\pi_{4}(SU(2)) = \mathbb{Z}_{2}$ there are gauge transformations not continuously connected to the identity, under which the fermion integral of one doublet changes sign, so with an odd number of doublets the partition function and every gauge-invariant expectation value vanish \cite{Witten1982}. A consistent theory of this kind has an even number of left-handed doublets.
synthesis.imported-witten-global-su2-ano.technical: Besides the perturbative (triangle) anomalies there is a global one for the weak isospin group: a single left-handed doublet, or any odd number of them, makes the theory ill defined, because a topologically nontrivial gauge transformation flips the sign of the fermion integral. Each Standard Model generation has four doublets (three colours of quark and one lepton), so the condition holds for any number of generations.
synthesis.imported-witten-global-su2-ano.lay: Witten found that a theory with the weak force acting on an odd number of left-handed particle pairs cannot be consistent, whatever else it contains. Each family of ordinary matter has four such pairs, so any number of families passes this test; it cannot be used to fix how many families there are.

imported_from.citation: E. Witten, An SU(2) anomaly, Phys. Lett. B 117 (1982), no. 5, 324--328.

synthesis.joint-clifford-clause-is-a-kle.formal:
Read numbers in $\mathrm{span}\{1, I_{4}\}$. Let $V = F \otimes \Lambda^{\bullet}W$ be the composite space of Premise \claimref{standard-model.slot-module-hypothesis}(a) with fermionic slot module $F = \Lambda^{\bullet}D$, $D$ the slot doublet; let $a_{i} = a(u_{i}) \otimes 1$ ($i = 1, 2$) be the slot annihilators, $b_{p} = 1 \otimes b(t_{p})$ ($p = 1, 2, 3$) the pair annihilators, $(-1)^{k}$ the pair parity, $(-1)^{N} = (-1)^{n + k}$ the grading, and $\tilde a_{i} = a_{i}(-1)^{k}$ the Klein-twisted slot operators.
\begin{enumerate}
\item[(i)] \emph{(Same slot data; proved.)} The $\tilde a_{i}$ satisfy the same canonical anticommutation relations as the $a_{i}$, transform in the same way under $U(2) \times U(3)$, and on $F_{n} \otimes \Lambda^{k}W$ have $\tilde a_{i}^{\dagger} = (-1)^{k}a_{i}^{\dagger}$, so clause (G) holds for one set exactly when it holds for the other.
\item[(ii)] \emph{(Opposite relation to the pairs; proved.)} The $a_{i}$ commute with every $b_{p}$, $b_{p}^{\dagger}$; the $\tilde a_{i}$ anticommute with them. So $\tilde a_{1}, \tilde a_{2}, b_{1}, b_{2}, b_{3}$ satisfy the canonical anticommutation relations of one system of five modes, and their real Majorana combinations, five of square $+1$ and five of square $-1$, generate $\Cl(5,5)$ on $V$, whose span over $\mathrm{span}\{1, I_{4}\}$ is the $\Cl(10)$ of clause (f).
\item[(iii)] \emph{(Convention-free operators; proved.)} The $21$ split-preserving bivectors (the $6$ slot-slot and $15$ pair-pair Majorana bivectors, the Pati-Salam algebra of clause (CPT)) and the grading $(-1)^{N}$, which anticommutes with $a_{i}$, $\tilde a_{i}$ and $b_{p}$ alike, are the same operators in both conventions.
\item[(iv)] \emph{(Uniqueness; proved.)} If an operator $K$ on $V$ commutes with every $a_{i}$, $a_{i}^{\dagger}$ and the $a_{i}K$ anticommute with every pair operator and satisfy the canonical anticommutation relations, then $K = c(-1)^{k}$ with $c$ a unit of $\mathrm{span}\{1, I_{4}\}$ (a phase from the centre of the slot $U(2)$), and $c = \pm 1$ if $K$ is an involution.
\item[(v)] \emph{(Consequence; proved on $V$.)} Clause (f) holds on $V$ for every $F \cong \Lambda^{\bullet}D$, canonically up to that unit: it is a convention on $V$ (the $24$ cross bivectors depend on the convention, but the residual sign acts on them by $\mathrm{Ad}$ of the slot parity, an element of $\mathrm{Spin}(10)$, so the $\mathrm{Spin}(10)$ of clause (f) is canonical), and the qualifier of clause (CPT) ``when the slot module is fermionic, so that clause (f) applies'' adds no condition beyond $F \cong \Lambda^{\bullet}D$. The clause keeps content only relative to slot operators given in advance, for instance as tower elements (the setting of \claimref{synthesis.even-slots-need-a-spectator-generator}(iii)), which is not addressed.
\end{enumerate}
The twist is the replacement $s_{i} \mapsto s_{i}\Gamma_{W}$ of \claimref{synthesis.even-slots-need-a-spectator-generator}(iii), the commuting-copies device of \claimref{tower.commuting-copies} read backwards. In the floor $\Cl(5,5)$ of \claimref{synthesis.even-slots-need-a-spectator-generator}, with the modes as null pairs of vectors, the twisted operators are the vectors themselves, the untwisted ones are the vectors times the pair parity $\Gamma_{W} = e_{2}f_{2}e_{3}f_{3}e_{4}f_{4}$, a single blade, and (iv) is a count of blades with the commutation form of \claimref{synthesis.blade-square-signs-f2-quadratic-form}(ii). Transport-absent.
synthesis.joint-clifford-clause-is-a-kle.technical: Clause (f) of the slot-module hypothesis asks that the slot and pair operators of a composite form one system of five fermionic modes, each slot operator anticommuting with each pair operator. On the tensor-product space $V = F \otimes \Lambda^{\bullet}W$ the natural slot operators commute with the pair operators instead. Multiplying them by the pair parity $(-1)^{k}$, the Klein transformation, turns commuting into anticommuting while keeping their anticommutation relations, their $U(2) \times U(3)$ behaviour and their images, so generation is unaffected. Everything the hypothesis asks of the chirality is the same in both conventions: the slot-slot and pair-pair bivectors (the Pati-Salam algebra) and the grading by the total mode number. The twist is unique: a factor commuting with the slot operators and making them anticommute with the pairs is a unit times $(-1)^{k}$, because it then commutes with all operators on $V$. In geometric algebra the five modes are null pairs of vectors in $\Cl(5,5)$, the twisted slot operators are those vectors, and the pair parity is the single blade $e_{2}f_{2}e_{3}f_{3}e_{4}f_{4}$; uniqueness is then a count with the two-element-field commutation form of blades. So on $V$ clause (f) is a convention, not a premise; it would carry content only for slot operators fixed in advance, for instance as tower elements, which this result does not treat. Transport-absent.
synthesis.joint-clifford-clause-is-a-kle.lay: The series builds each quark or lepton from two kinds of ingredients, slots and pairs, and one of its assumptions says that the two kinds behave as a single family of fermions, swapping sign whenever one of each is exchanged. This result shows that, on the particle's own space of states, this costs nothing: if slot and pair operators are first written so that they ignore each other, a standard trick (multiplying each slot operator by a sign that counts the pairs) makes them behave as one family, changes nothing else that the theory uses, and is the only way to do it up to an overall sign. The assumption only matters if the slot operators are fixed in advance by something else, such as the deeper tower of the theory.
flags: the kill condition was not run over the future cone of the slot-module hypothesis: results that use the slot operators as given tower elements could still give clause (f) content; on V itself it has none

proofs.main:
\emph{Notation.} Numbers are read in $\mathrm{span}\{1, I_{4}\}$ (conventions); $D$ is the slot doublet, $F = \Lambda^{\bullet}D$, $V = F \otimes \Lambda^{\bullet}W$; $a_{i} = a(u_{i}) \otimes 1$ ($u_{1}, u_{2}$ an orthonormal basis of $D$, $a^{\dagger}(u) = u \wedge$), $b_{p} = 1 \otimes b(t_{p})$ ($t_{1}, t_{2}, t_{3}$ an orthonormal basis of $W$), $(-1)^{k} = 1 \otimes (-1)^{\deg}$ the pair parity, $(-1)^{N} = (-1)^{n}(-1)^{k}$, and $\tilde a_{i} = a_{i}(-1)^{k}$. Products of operators on a tensor product: $(X \otimes Y)(X' \otimes Y') = XX' \otimes YY'$, so operators on different factors commute.

\emph{Step 1 (realisation in geometric algebra).} Take the floor $\Cl(5,5)$ of \claimref{synthesis.even-slots-need-a-spectator-generator}: generators $e_{k}$ ($e_{k}^{2} = 1$), $f_{k}$ ($f_{k}^{2} = -1$), $k = 0, \dots, 4$, null pairs $v_{k} = \tfrac12(e_{k} + f_{k})$, $w_{k} = \tfrac12(e_{k} - f_{k})$ with $v_{k}w_{l} + w_{l}v_{k} = \delta_{kl}$ and all other anticommutators zero, modes $0, 1$ the slots and $2, 3, 4$ the pairs, vacuum the null blade $\Omega = w_{0}\cdots w_{4}$. The $32$ states $v_{K}v_{J}\Omega$ ($v_{K}$ an ordered product of pair creators, $v_{J}$ of slot creators) are independent and span the Fock ideal; identify $v_{K}v_{J}\Omega$ with $u_{J} \otimes t_{K}$. A pair vector, acting from the left, passes no slot vector, so it acts as $1 \otimes b$; a slot vector passes the $k$ pair creators of $v_{K}$, so it acts as $a \otimes (-1)^{k}$: the vectors $v_{i}, w_{i}$ ($i = 0, 1$) are the twisted $\tilde a^{\dagger}_{i}, \tilde a_{i}$, and the untwisted ones are $v_{i}\Gamma_{W}$, $w_{i}\Gamma_{W}$ with $\Gamma_{W} = \prod_{p}(1 - 2v_{p}w_{p})$, the pair parity, as in clause (iii) of that result; the device is the commuting-copies twist of \claimref{tower.commuting-copies} read backwards. Since $2v_{p}w_{p} = \tfrac12(e_{p} + f_{p})(e_{p} - f_{p}) = 1 - e_{p}f_{p}$, $1 - 2v_{p}w_{p} = e_{p}f_{p}$ and $\Gamma_{W} = e_{2}f_{2}e_{3}f_{3}e_{4}f_{4}$ is a single blade, $\Gamma_{W}^{2} = 1$, commuting with the slot vectors and anticommuting with the six pair vectors. Over $\mathrm{span}\{1, I_{4}\}$, $I_{4}$ commuting with all ten generators, $\Cl(5,5)$ spans $\mathrm{End}(V)$.

\emph{Step 2 ((i) and (ii)).} $\Gamma_{W}$ commutes with $a_{i}$, $a_{i}^{\dagger}$ and squares to $1$, so $\tilde a_{i}\tilde a_{j}^{\dagger} + \tilde a_{j}^{\dagger}\tilde a_{i} = a_{i}a_{j}^{\dagger} + a_{j}^{\dagger}a_{i} = \delta_{ij}$ and likewise for the other anticommutators. $A \otimes \Lambda^{\bullet}B$ preserves the pair degree, so it commutes with $(-1)^{k}$ and $\tilde a_{i}$ transforms as $a_{i}$ does. On $F_{n} \otimes \Lambda^{k}W$, $\tilde a_{i}^{\dagger} = (-1)^{k}a_{i}^{\dagger}$, so the creation maps have the same images and clause (G) holds for one set exactly when it holds for the other. The $a_{i}$ act on the first factor and the $b_{p}$ on the second, so they commute; $(-1)^{k}$ anticommutes with $b_{p}$ and $b_{p}^{\dagger}$, so $\tilde a_{i}b_{p} = -b_{p}\tilde a_{i}$ (in $\Cl(5,5)$: distinct vectors anticommute). Hence $\tilde a_{1}, \tilde a_{2}, b_{1}, b_{2}, b_{3}$ satisfy the canonical anticommutation relations of one system of five modes, and the real Majorana combinations $\tilde a + \tilde a^{\dagger}$, $\tilde a - \tilde a^{\dagger}$, $b + b^{\dagger}$, $b - b^{\dagger}$ are the ten vectors $e_{k}$, $f_{k}$, generating $\Cl(5,5)$; its span over $\mathrm{span}\{1, I_{4}\}$ is the $\Cl(10)$ of clause (f), with no imaginary unit needed for the Majorana of square $-1$.

\emph{Step 3 ((iii)).} For two slot operators $x, y$, $(x\Gamma_{W})(y\Gamma_{W}) = xy\,\Gamma_{W}^{2} = xy$; so every slot-slot bilinear, in particular the $\binom{4}{2} = 6$ slot Majorana bivectors, is the same element in both conventions. The pair operators are not twisted, so the $\binom{6}{2} = 15$ pair Majorana bivectors are the same too: the $21$ split-preserving bivectors of clause (CPT), the Pati-Salam algebra (\claimref{standard-model.automorphisms-preserve-slot-pair-split-are}, cited for the name only), do not depend on the convention. $\Gamma_{W}$ commutes with every slot-slot and pair-pair bilinear, the generators of $\uu(2) \oplus \uu(3)$ and the pair creation and annihilation bilinears among them. The grading $(-1)^{N} = \prod_{k=0}^{4}e_{k}f_{k}$ anticommutes with every one of the ten vectors and commutes with $\Gamma_{W}$, so it anticommutes with $a_{i}$, $\tilde a_{i}$ and $b_{p}$ alike: the grading form of clause (CPT) does not depend on the convention either.

\emph{Step 4 ((iv), uniqueness).} Let $K$ commute with every $a_{i}$, $a_{i}^{\dagger}$, and let $a_{i}K$ anticommute with every $b_{p}$, $b_{p}^{\dagger}$ and satisfy the canonical anticommutation relations. For a pair operator $\beta$, $a_{i}K\beta + \beta a_{i}K = a_{i}(K\beta + \beta K)$, and likewise with $a_{i}^{\dagger}$; adding $a_{i}^{\dagger}$ times the first to $a_{i}$ times the second gives $K\beta + \beta K = 0$. So $K(-1)^{k}$ commutes with every pair operator and every slot operator. The slot operators generate $\mathrm{End}(F) \otimes 1$ and the pair operators $1 \otimes \mathrm{End}(\Lambda^{\bullet}W)$ (the Fock representations of the canonical anticommutation relations are irreducible), which together generate $\mathrm{End}(V)$; so $K(-1)^{k}$ is a number $c \in \mathrm{span}\{1, I_{4}\}$, and the relation $(a_{i}K)(a_{i}K)^{\dagger} + (a_{i}K)^{\dagger}(a_{i}K) = |c|^{2} = 1$ makes $c$ a unit; $c = \pm 1$ when $K$ is an involution or a real element of the floor. A unit $c$ is a phase that the centre of the slot $U(2)$ already supplies. In the realisation the same follows by counting blades with the commutation form of \claimref{synthesis.blade-square-signs-f2-quadratic-form}(ii): blades $e_{S}$, $e_{T}$ anticommute exactly when $b(S, T) = |S||T| + |S \cap T| = 1 \pmod 2$; the conditions are diagonal in the blade basis, and with $P = \{e_{2}, e_{3}, e_{4}, f_{2}, f_{3}, f_{4}\}$, $b(S, \{x\}) = |S| + [x \in S] = 1$ for all $x \in P$ forces $S \supseteq P$ with $|S|$ even or $S \cap P = \emptyset$ with $|S|$ odd, and commuting with the untwisted slot Majoranas $e_{S'}$, $S' = \{y\} \cup P$, forces $[y \in S] = |S| + |S \cap P| \pmod 2$ for the four slot generators $y$; the first case gives $S = P$, the second would need all four slot generators in $S$ with $|S| = 4$ odd. So $K \in \mathrm{span}\{\Gamma_{W}\}$.

\emph{Step 5 (the reading; (v)).} By Steps 2 to 4, on $V$ the operators required by clause (f) exist whenever $F \cong \Lambda^{\bullet}D$, namely the Klein-twisted slot operators, unique up to a unit; every operator the clause produces ($\Cl(10)$, $\mathrm{Spin}(10)$, the $24$ cross bivectors) is an operator on $V$ built from them, and everything clause (CPT) asks of the convention is convention-free. The $24$ cross bivectors do depend on the convention (only the twisted operators give $\mathrm{Spin}(10)$); the residual sign $c = -1$ acts on them by $\mathrm{Ad}$ of the slot parity $(-1)^{n} = e_{0}f_{0}e_{1}f_{1}$ (of reverse norm $1$, the central element $-1$ of the slot $U(2)$, an element of $\mathrm{Spin}(10)$), which negates the slot Majoranas and fixes the pair ones, so the $\mathrm{Spin}(10)$ of clause (f) is canonical as a subgroup. So on $V$ clause (f) is a choice of convention with no content of its own. It keeps content only relative to an embedding of slot operators given in advance, for instance as tower elements, where the question is whether the given operators are the twisted or the untwisted ones; this is the setting of \claimref{synthesis.even-slots-need-a-spectator-generator}(iii), which already makes the replacement $s_{i} \mapsto s_{i}\Gamma_{W}$, and it is not addressed here. The checks verify Steps 1 to 4 exactly in $\Cl(5,5)$, including the commutation form against the products for all $1024$ blades.
